rows.notes: Conceptual/policy comparison paper (HESS special issue) that posits efficiency, scale and sectoral 'paradoxes' and illustrates them with three case descriptions (Limari, Imperial Valley, Guadiana) built from census/statistical compilations and cited work. No original experiment, survey or model runs. The rebound-type statements (drip share rising to 60% while irrigated area grew 40,000 to 60,000 ha in Limari, Table 1; Guadiana savings reused for area expansion) are descriptive associations from secondary statistics or are attributed to AEVAL (2010) and Lopez-Gunn et al. (2012), not the authors' own result. If a reader treats the compiled census trends as own observational data, the paper would still offer only a descriptive, single-method, uncertainty-free association, with the authors noting records do not allow inference of the pre-efficiency situation.

Same conceptual paper. The link between drip conversion, reduced return flows and ecosystem water (scale paradox) is asserted conceptually (Fig. 1 framework drawing on Perry 2011) and illustrated with secondary descriptions: Limari outlet streamflow exceeding 5 m3/s only 35% of time in the lower reach (Fig. 3) with the authors explicitly stating the record cannot show conditions before the efficiency/area increase; Salton Sea inflow decline cited to Case III et al. (2013); Guadiana ecosystem degradation cited to Blanco-Gutierrez et al. No own measurement of return flows or ecosystem effects under drip versus flood.

notes: Full text appears complete. The paper is a perspective/synthesis with illustrative case examples; its only quasi-original analysis is a streamflow-precipitation comparison for the Limari outlet (Fig. 3), which the authors themselves say cannot be linked to the irrigation efficiency change. Rated as non-primary; if a reader classed it as primary observational work, Q2 would remain weak because effects are described from secondary statistics and cited studies rather than tested.
